sentences: A round moon is caught at the tip of a plum branch that shoots straight up.
Below it a thick trunk holds firm, and here and there on the twigs hang a few blossoms and buds.
This is Plum Blossoms in Moonlight, painted by Eo Mongryong, a scholar-painter of the mid-Joseon period.
It is painted in ink alone on silk, 119.
1 centimetres high and 53 centimetres wide.
It now belongs to the National Museum of Korea in Seoul, and it is often called by its Korean name, Wolmaedo, the moon and plum picture.
Look first at the moon near the top.
A branch rises straight through the middle of the picture and almost touches it.
The whole composition is built from just two things, the moon and the plum, so the empty silk around them simply becomes the night sky.
Now look down at the thick trunk.
Its ends are all broken off, as if it had weathered many hard winters.
The painter used a dry brush, so the pale ground shows through the strokes, a technique called flying white.
The rough, split lines of ink show the years the old tree has endured.
Come closer to the blossoms on the branch.
There are not many, and open flowers mix with tight buds.
The stamens and the little moss dots along the branches are touched in one by one with dark ink, each dot separate, giving the quiet picture a small pulse of movement.
Eo Mongryong was born around 1566 and died in 1617.
He came from a family of scholar-officials: his grandfather had been a minister and his father a county magistrate, and in 1604 he himself served as magistrate of Jincheon.
His pen name was Seolgok, Snowy Valley.
He made his name with the plum alone.
Together with Yi Jeong, famous for bamboo, and Hwang Jipjung, famous for grapes, he was called one of the Three Masters of his day.
Yang Hao, a visitor from Ming China, praised the high quality of his plum paintings but regretted that no branch hung downwards.
Zhu Zhifan was harsher, saying that because every calyx pointed upwards the flowers looked like apricot blossoms.
Scholars today read these mixed reviews as evidence that Joseon plum painting had found a character of its own, different from China's.
Pairing the moon with plum blossoms was a favourite theme of many painters of the time, because plum flowers were thought to look whiter and lovelier in moonlight.
The philosopher Yi Hwang left a poem about leaning on a mountain window at night, watching a round moon rise to the tip of a plum branch.
His spare, upright plum paintings went on to shape the work of the next generation, including Jo Sok, Heo Mok and Jo Jiun.
Step back and look again.
A broken trunk, a straight branch, a few flowers and a round moon: that is all.
Tonight, if the moon rises outside your window, imagine what you would like to place beneath it.
